Members of the genus Chaetodon typically produce pelagic eggs that hatch into small, endotrophic larvae reliant on endogenous yolk reserves for several days following eclosion. For the Diagonal butterflyfish, the duration of the embryonic period is brief, with hatching occurring after approximately 7 days [ab = approximately 7 days] when water temperatures are maintained at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. This rapid developmental pace is characteristic of many tropical butterflyfishes and matches values reported for the congener Chaetodon larvatus under similar thermal regimes. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva is minute; based on an egg diameter of 0.75 mm, the calculated wet weight at birth is approximately 0.00023 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00023 grams], a mass that reflects the limited volume of yolk resources available to support the endotrophic phase. This initial mass, though tiny, must sustain the prolarva until mouth opening and the onset of first exogenous feeding, a trophic switch that typically occurs within a few days post-hatching in warm-water teleosts.

As the pelagic larva grows and undergoes flexion, it begins to acquire the morphological characteristics of a juvenile butterflyfish. The transition from a planktonic to a benthic, reef-associated existence occurs through larval metamorphosis and subsequent settlement, after which the post-settlement juvenile enters a period of rapid somatic growth. For Chaetodon fasciatus, the onset of sexual maturation, or puberty, is attained at a total length of approximately 11 centimeters [Lp = approximately 11 centimeters]. This length marks the point at which gametogenesis commences and the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis becomes fully activated. The corresponding wet weight at this pubertal stage, derived from the species length-weight relationship, is estimated at around 30.5 grams [Wwp = around 30.5 grams]. This body mass represents a considerable increase from the hatchling weight, reflecting the accumulation of somatic tissue and lipid reserves necessary to support the energetic demands of gonad maturation and eventual reproductive activity.

Field surveys and growth curve analyses indicate that the Diagonal butterflyfish continues to increase in size well beyond the onset of maturity, eventually reaching an ultimate total length of 22 centimeters [Li = 22 centimeters]. This maximum size, recorded from the oldest and largest individuals within sampled populations, defines the species asymptotic length and represents an important life-history parameter. At this terminal size, the corresponding ultimate wet weight is calculated to be approximately 244 grams [Wwi = approximately 244 grams], a body mass consistent with the general allometric scaling patterns observed across the Chaetodontidae. The relationship between length and weight in this species follows a power function with an exponent near 3.00, indicating isometric growth where body proportions remain relatively stable throughout the juvenile and adult phases. This ultimate body size influences a range of ecological attributes, including the species vulnerability to predation, its dietary breadth, and its competitive interactions with other coral reef fishes.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Chaetodon fasciatus provides a measure of relative gonad mass. At a water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the average gonadosomatic index was approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%]. This estimate, which draws on comparative data from the closely related species Chaetodon larvatus, suggests that ovarian and testicular mass collectively represent about six percent of the total body weight during peak spawning periods. Such a level of allocation is typical for iteroparous coral reef fishes that spawn repeatedly over an extended breeding season, balancing the energetic costs of gamete production against the demands of somatic maintenance, foraging, and territorial defense. The index may vary seasonally in response to fluctuations in food availability and water temperature.

Longevity data for the Diagonal butterflyfish document a maximum lifespan of approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years] under natural conditions in the Red Sea, calculated from field-based age estimations using otolith microincrement analysis at a stable water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. This extended lifespan, equating to roughly 7300 days, is relatively high for a teleost of this body size and places Chaetodon fasciatus among the longer-lived members of the family Chaetodontidae. The species' slow pace of life, characterized by a delayed onset of reproduction relative to many smaller reef fishes, is likely linked to the predictable but moderate productivity of its coral-dominated foraging habitats. Such a life-history strategy, combining protracted somatic growth with a long reproductive tenure, allows individuals to spread reproductive effort across numerous spawning seasons, thereby buffering against years of poor recruitment or environmental disturbance. Senescence in this species presumably occurs through progressive physiological decline.

A comprehensive understanding of the life history of the Diagonal butterflyfish also requires consideration of its reproductive strategy in the context of the coral reef environment. The species is iteroparous, spawning multiple times over its extended lifespan, which allows for repeated reproductive events that buffer against environmental stochasticity. The relatively late attainment of sexual maturity, marked by a total length of 11 centimeters, ensures that individuals have reached a sufficient body size to support the costs of reproduction. This life-history pattern, combining a prolonged juvenile phase with a long adult reproductive tenure, is typical of many Chaetodontidae and reflects the ecological constraints of life on coral reefs.
